title: Vz-GAL Dusty Star-Forming Galaxies: Revisiting the CO–H2 Conversion Factor Tension

paper.title: V z -GAL Dusty Star-Forming Galaxies: Revisiting the CO–H 2 Conversion Factor Tension
paper.abstract: Abstract The CO luminosity-to-H 2 mass conversion factor ( α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} ) remains a debated uncertainty in determining molecular gas masses of high-redshift dusty star-forming galaxies (DSFGs). Dynamical mass constraints have often favored α CO = 0.8 \alpha_{\rm CO}=0.8 M ⊙ ​ ( K ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ pc 2 ) − 1 \rm M_{\odot}~{(K~km~{s}^{-1}~{pc}^{2})}^{-1} , whereas dust- and radiative-transfer-based methods imply higher values. We revisit this “tension” using the largest homogeneous sample of 21 unlensed z ∼ 1 − 4 z\sim 1-4 DSFGs, with securely measured CO(1–0) luminosities from the VLA V z -GAL survey and resolved ( ∼ 0.1 ′′ \sim{0.1}^{\prime\prime} ) ALMA 1 mm dust continuum imaging. For 12 galaxies with robust modeling constraints, we derive molecular gas masses using dust spectral energy distribution modeling and the TUNER LVG framework, adopting a solar-metallicity gas-to-dust mass ratio of 100. Although not fully independent due to shared assumptions on dust properties, these approaches yield mutually consistent gas masses corresponding to α CO ∼ 1.5 − 11.5 \alpha_{\rm CO}\sim 1.5-11.5 M ⊙ ​ ( K ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ pc 2 ) − 1 \rm M_{\odot}~{(K~km~{s}^{-1}~{pc}^{2})}^{-1} , with a median near the Galactic α CO = 4.3 \alpha_{\rm CO}=4.3 M ⊙ ​ ( K ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ pc 2 ) − 1 \rm M_{\odot}~{(K~km~{s}^{-1}~{pc}^{2})}^{-1} . Isotropic virial dynamical masses agree with these gas masses when realistic molecular gas sizes are adopted, while our proposed “mixed” (rotating, pressure-supported, thick-disk) estimator systematically underestimates dynamical masses, producing low α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} limits. Using GN20 ( z = 4.055 z=4.055 ) as a case study, we show that resolved gas geometry and kinematics reconcile the discrepancy with LVG-derived α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} . Our results suggest that current data do not require α CO = 0.8 ​ M ⊙ ​ ( K ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ pc 2 ) − 1 \alpha_{\rm CO}=0.8~\rm M_{\odot}~(K~km~s^{-1}~pc^{2})^{-1} , and intermediate to near-Galactic values remain dynamically viable given uncertainties in gas geometry, dust properties, and gas-to-dust ratios. Further progress in calibrating α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} in the early universe will require resolved molecular gas observations, physically motivated ISM modeling, and stringent constraints on dust properties.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: Cold molecular gas is a fundamental component in the formation and evolution of galaxies across cosmic time [ 85 , 80 , 100 , 103 ] . Commonly traced via 12 C 16 O — hereafter, CO — rotational transitions, it both fuels star formation and serves as a sensitive probe of galactic gas dynamics. CO(1–0), with ν rest = 115.271 \rm\nu_{rest}=115.271 GHz, is the ground-state rotational transition and can be excited even in the most extended, cold gas reservoirs. CO(1–0) line luminosities, L CO ⁡ ( 1 − 0 ) ′ L^{\prime}_{\rm CO(1-0)} (in units of K ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ pc 2 \rm K~km~{s}^{-1}~{pc}^{2} ) are, therefore, commonly used to derive total molecular gas masses ( M H 2 M_{\rm H_{2}} ) via the CO–H 2 conversion factor [ 90 , α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} in units of M ⊙ ​ ( K ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ pc 2 ) − 1 \rm M_{\odot}~{(K~km~{s}^{-1}~{pc}^{2})}^{-1} ; see] . M H 2 ​ [ M ⊙ ] = α CO ​ L CO ⁡ ( 1 − 0 ) ′ M_{\rm H_{2}}\,{\rm[M_{\odot}]}=\alpha_{\rm CO}\,\,L^{\prime}_{\rm CO(1-0)} (1) Within the Milky Way and nearby main-sequence galaxies, α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} is known to vary with local physical conditions, including temperature, density, and metallicity [ 67 , 59 , e.g.,] . However, direct, non-dynamical estimates of the α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} conversion factor in the local universe are themselves subject to significant systematic uncertainties. Calibrations based on γ \gamma -ray emission, visual and infrared extinction, X-ray absorption, dust emission, and isotopologue measurements generally agree at ∼ \sim 15–25% level, but exhibit an overall spread approaching a factor of about 2 in some environments [ 66 , see e.g.,] . Importantly, these differences are not purely statistical but appear to be systematically offset between methods, suggesting that residual physical and methodological uncertainties remain even in nearby systems where such calibrations are most applicable. On galaxy-integrated scales, additional uncertainty is expected due to the optical thickness of the low- J CO transitions, which can produce intrinsic variations in CO emissivity across different gas phases and environments [ 8 ] . Such effects are already evident in resolved observations of local molecular clouds and complexes [ 63 , e.g.,] . On the other hand, local ultra-luminous infrared galaxies or ULIRGs and high- z dusty star-forming galaxies (DSFGs) rarely have direct measurements of α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} . Instead, their α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} is typically inferred from unresolved, global CO observations and indirect constraints, relying on assumptions about gas geometry, excitation conditions, dynamics, gravitationally supported motions, and virialization that may break down in extreme star-forming environments [ 8 , 39 ] . A long-standing result from these approaches is that submillimeter-bright dusty systems across redshifts appear to convert gas into stars more rapidly than coeval main-sequence galaxies, implying short depletion times and highly efficient star formation such as that seen in local ULIRGs/mergers [ 38 , 5 , 46 , 76 , e.g.,] . In the same systems, masses inferred from dynamical constraints using integrated CO linewidths are often lower than the molecular gas masses obtained from CO luminosity when adopting a Milky Way-calibrated α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} , implying that a systematically lower inferred CO–H 2 conversion factor is appropriate for ULIRGs and DSFGs [ 27 , 2 , e.g.,] . This discrepancy is commonly referred to as the “ α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} tension”. A key open question is whether the apparent tension between galaxy-integrated molecular gas masses inferred from CO luminosities and dynamical constraints reflects genuine variations in the physical conversion factor across populations or instead arises from observational limitations. While studies of nearby molecular clouds and ULIRGs generally benefit from well-constrained dynamics, remaining discrepancies there may instead reflect assumptions about the physical state of the gas (e.g., virial equilibrium or cloud structure). In contrast, high- z DSFGs are affected by substantially larger observational uncertainties. The absence of integrated CO(1–0) measurements in many studies introduces uncertainties associated with gas excitation corrections. Even when such data are available, complex kinematic structures — including rotation, turbulence, inflows/outflows, and merger-driven motions — are generally reduced to a single integrated linewidth. In addition, dynamical mass estimates depend on source sizes, geometry, and inclination, parameters that are often poorly constrained, thereby compounding the overall uncertainty. These quantities are typically inferred from resolved dust continuum morphology because directly imaging the cold molecular gas at comparable resolution remains observationally challenging. Altogether, these may systematically bias gas mass and dynamical estimates, making it difficult to determine whether the inferred global, low α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} values in high- z DSFGs are intrinsic or observationally driven. Spatially resolved observations of inherently faint CO(1–0) offer a direct way to break these degeneracies by independently constraining gas extent and kinematics for high- z DSFGs. However, such studies remain limited at high redshift due to sensitivity constraints. They are typically restricted to the brightest or strongly lensed galaxies and quasars [ 77 , 96 , 87 , e.g.,] , where interpretations may be affected by additional uncertainties from lensing reconstruction models. Existing high-resolution CO(1–0) and CO(2–1) studies of unlensed high- z DSFGs [ 39 , e.g.,] remain limited to only a handful of objects (e.g., GN20 at z ∼ 4 z\sim 4 ; Hodge et al. 49 ) and often lack the sensitivity required for robust dynamical modeling. Consequently, they have not yet determined whether the apparent low α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} values in high- z DSFGs arise primarily from observational limitations or reflect genuine physical variations. Discrepancies between the molecular gas mass estimates and dynamical constraints remain even when masses are inferred from integrated [CII] or (typically optically thin) [CI] observations 1 1 1 Assuming all C + or C is directly related to star formation, i.e., no formation due to shock compression. , lacking a systematic comparison of conversion factors across various tracers for large samples of DSFGs [ 29 , 32 , e.g.,] . This motivates a re-examination of the apparent α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} tension in high- z DSFGs, where observational limitations are likely to play a much larger role than in nearby systems. Quantifying the impact of unresolved kinematics and uncertain source sizes is essential for determining whether these observational biases largely drive the low conversion factors inferred for current high- z statistical samples or whether a residual discrepancy remains after improved dynamical constraints are obtained. A previous study of homogeneously selected unlensed, high- z DSFGs reports 11 robust CO(1–0) detections [ 38 ] . Further, a handful of additional CO(1–0) studies of unlensed galaxies exist, such as [ 15 , 55 , 88 , 58 ] . To address limitations arising from heterogeneous selection effects and limited statistics, the VLA V z -GAL CO(1--0) large program 2 2 2 vzgal.uni-koeln.de [ 93 , 76 ] has studied CO(1–0) emission in 106 Herschel/SPIRE 500 μ \mu m-selected high- z DSFGs. These 106 sources were selected from a parent sample of 135 DSFGs detected in higher- J CO lines and far-infrared continuum by the NOEMA z -GAL survey [ 22 ] . In this paper, we focus on the unlensed sources identified at z = 1 − 6 z=1-6 within the V z -GAL sample. In Section II , we describe the identification of the target sample and available data. In Section III , we analyze the data to infer resolved dust sizes and inclination angles. We also derive their gas masses using two complementary methods, one using dust spectral energy distribution modeling and another involving a large velocity gradient model [ 104 , 10 , LVG; see] . Section IV explores an isotropic virial and a rotational thick-disk estimator of dynamical masses for DSFGs, and compares them to the molecular gas masses. 3 3 3 The dynamical constraints explored in this work should be interpreted in the context of a non-negligible intrinsic uncertainty floor in the standard CO–H 2 conversion factors, even in the local universe, alongside observational and modeling uncertainties in the gas mass and dynamical measurements. Section V discusses the inferences of the comparison in the context of the α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} tension, followed by a summary in Section VI . Throughout the work, we use a spatially flat Lambda Cold Dark Matter ( Λ \Lambda CDM) cosmology with H 0 {H}_{\mathrm{0}} = 67.4 km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 \mathrm{km}\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1} and Ω M {\Omega}_{\mathrm{M}} = 0.315 [ 75 ] . Unless otherwise stated, all uncertainties on median values reported in this paper are given as the median absolute deviation (MAD).

sections.heading: II.1 Sample Selection: V z -GAL Unlensed DSFGs
sections.text: The high- z dusty galaxies in the V z -GAL sample are originally selected based on S 500 ​ μ ​ m > 80 S_{500\mu{\rm m}}>80 mJy [ 76 , see Figure 1 of] . They have robust positions and redshifts based on higher- J CO line observations from the NOEMA z -GAL program [ 22 ] , which consists of 135 sources with S 500 ​ μ ​ m > 80 S_{500\mu{\rm m}}>80 mJy selected from ∼ 700 \sim 700 deg 2 of the largest fields observed with the Herschel/SPIRE instrument. Assuming optically thin dust emission, Ismail et al. [54] modeled the integrated dust spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of the sample, while Berta et al. [5] studied the gas properties. Recent ALMA 1 mm (rest-frame ∼ \sim 300 μ \mu m at the median z ∼ 2.3 z\sim 2.3 of the sample) dust continuum observations at ∼ 0.1 ′′ \sim{0.1}^{\prime\prime} (Bakx et al., in prep.) show the resolved morphologies of these dusty sources, which are used here along with the HST/F110W imaging [ 11 ] , Subaru/HSC, or Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) imaging of foreground objects to separate lensed from unlensed sources. For this paper, we visually classify a V z -GAL galaxy as gravitationally lensed if it satisfies one or both of the following criteria (see Figure 1 ): (i) the ALMA dust continuum exhibits clear lensing signatures, such as extended morphologies with arcs, rings, or Einstein crosses, and/or (ii) a foreground object is present along the line of sight in the HST imaging that could plausibly act as a lens for the DSFG in the background. Galaxies that instead display compact dust emission peak(s) and lack any evident foreground lensing source are classified as unlensed DSFGs (see also Appendix § \lx@sectionsign VII.1 ). Figure 1 : Classification of the V z -GAL high- z dusty galaxies as lensed or unlensed sources, their CO(1–0) line fluxes and redshift distribution. We find that DSFGs at lower line fluxes show a higher fraction of unlensed galaxies, as expected. We find 19 Herschel fields with 27 isolated dusty galaxies (Table 1 , Figure 2 ) and 14 fields (18 sources, Appendix VII.1 ) containing multiple sources in the ALMA dust maps that are unlensed. In the latter fields, sources are close enough to each other to remain blended in the V z -GAL data. Hence, these sources are not discussed further in this work, which focuses on the individual galaxies. Out of these DSFGs, 2/27 (HerBS-70W and HerBS-95W) fall on the edges of the available ALMA dust maps, and 3/27 have only tentative CO(1–0) detections (2 σ \sigma –3 σ \sigma , Table 1 ). Further, HerBS-171 ( z = 2.479 z=2.479 ) is not robustly resolved with the available ALMA data (see Table 1 ). After removing these 6/27 objects, our final sample consists of 21 unlensed V z -GAL galaxies at z ∼ 1 − 4 z\sim 1-4 . These galaxies represent the largest homogeneous CO(1–0) sample of unlensed DSFGs in the early universe. sections.heading: II.2 ALMA Continuum Observations
sections.text: Observed-frame 1 mm continuum in our target sample was observed using ALMA Band 7 across the years 2023 to 2025 (2022.1.00145.S, PI: Bakx; 2024.1.01570.S, PI: Algera; 2025.1.00326.S, PI: Bendo). The maximum baselines range from 2.5 to 3.7 km, with typically achieved angular resolutions across the 1 mm Band between 0.1 ′′ − 0.2 ′′ {0.1}^{\prime\prime}-{0.2}^{\prime\prime} or about 0.84–1.68 kpc at median z ∼ 2.3 z\sim 2.3 (Table 1 ). Each source was observed under excellent observing conditions, for a total on-source integration time of ∼ 3 \sim 3 min. Depending on the redshift of the source, these observations probe different rest-frame wavelengths (see Table 1 ). The Common Astronomy Software Application [ 69 , 17 , CASA ,] has been used to reduce and image the ALMA data; more details on this will be provided by Bakx et al. (in prep.). We show the resulting maps in Figure 2 . Further, Table 1 provides primary-beam-corrected continuum flux densities and signal-to-noise (S/N) ratios at the respective rest-frame wavelengths of each target. All the detections have peak S/N ratio of ≳ \gtrsim 10, with HerBS-187W ( z = 1.827 z=1.827 ; S/N ∼ \sim 5) as an exception.

sections.heading: II.3 V z -GAL CO(1–0) Measurements
sections.text: Unresolved measurements of the CO(1–0) emission-line fluxes for our targets were presented in the V z -GAL studies [ 93 , 76 ] . All the 21 DSFGs selected here have > 3 ​ σ >3\sigma detection of the CO(1–0) line. Table 2 summarizes their FWHM and CO(1–0) line luminosities adopted from the V z -GAL papers. The overall spread in CO(1–0) line luminosities of our sources is consistent with that found in the literature for high- z DSFGs or submillimeter galaxies (SMGs) [ 2 , 38 , e.g.,] . CO(1–0) emission for most of the 21 targets can be well described by a single Gaussian profile with an FWHM of 300 to 700 km s − 1 \rm{s}^{-1} . Similar linewidths have also been observed in the literature for other unlensed SMGs/DSFGs [ 15 , 38 , e.g.,] . A few of our systems, however, show more complex CO(1–0) line profiles (Appendix § \lx@sectionsign VII.2 ). • HeLMS-32C, HeLMS-50, HerBS-43a, and HerBS-43b show double-peaked CO(1–0) line profiles. All except HeLMS-50 are nearly symmetric, and the spatial distribution of dust emission in all of them appears compact. • HeLMS-50, HerBS-43a, HerBS-188, and HerBS-191 show broad (FWHM ≳ \gtrsim 1000 km s − 1 {\rm s}^{-1} ) CO(1–0) line profiles. Their resolved dust emission does not show any clear merger signatures. Moreover, HeLMS-50, HerBS-43a, HerBS-43b, and HerBS-191 exhibit dust radii larger than 3 kpc ( § \lx@sectionsign III.1.1 ), leading to their total dust extents spanning beyond ∼ \sim 6 kpc. For all systems displaying complex CO(1--0) line profiles, the lack of obvious merger signatures in the current ALMA dust-continuum maps, however, does not rule out ongoing or past merger activity, particularly if such features are obscured by projection effects. 4 4 4 We also expect that deeper, multi-array-configuration dust observations would further help reveal more extended dust emission in all sources.

sections.heading: III.1 Dust Morphology
sections.text: As mentioned in § \lx@sectionsign II.1 , all the selected targets show compact dust morphology in the ALMA maps (Figure 2 ). Their measured beam-deconvolved major- and minor-axis sizes, r major r_{\mathrm{major}} and r minor r_{\mathrm{minor}} , are reported in Table 1 , which are derived using 2D Gaussian fitting with CASA IMFIT . The beam position angles (PA) are also tabulated.

sections.heading: III.1.1 Dust Radii and Axis Ratios
sections.text: We assume that the dust is distributed in a circular, inclined disk-like morphology, whose size ( R dust R_{\rm dust} ) is thus best represented by the major axis size of the dust emission; i.e., R dust = r major {R}_{\mathrm{dust}}=r_{\mathrm{major}} . Most sources in our sample have dust-emitting radii between 1–3 kpc (Figure 3 ), with a sample median radius of 2.2 ± 0.4 2.2\pm 0.4 kpc. Only 5/21 sources (HeLMS-50, HerBS-43a, HerBS-43b, HerBS-70E, and HerBS-191) exhibit radii above 3 kpc. Among these, HerBS-191 is the most extended source with a dust-emitting radius ∼ \sim 7 kpc. Based on the minor and major axis sizes listed in Table 1 , we derive the observed axis ratios q = r minor / r major q=r_{\rm minor}/r_{\rm major} spanning 0.4–0.9, with a median value of 0.6 ± 0.1 0.6\pm 0.1 . The median axis ratio and overall range are comparable between 6/21 sources ( § \lx@sectionsign II.3 ) with complex CO(1–0) line profiles and the rest with a single Gaussian-like line profile. The observed range of axis ratios reveals a broad diversity in projected dust morphologies, from nearly circular to highly elongated.

sections.heading: III.1.2 Dust versus Cold Molecular Gas Sizes
sections.text: The median dust radius of 2.2 kpc for our sample is about 3 × 3\times lower than previously assumed [ 12 ] or previously observed [ 78 , 55 , 49 ] low- J CO radii of 7 kpc in the literature. For a given galaxy, the dust continuum size is expected to be lower than the cold gas size due to the radiative-transfer effects [ 14 , 10 , e.g.,] involving spatial variations in gas column density, temperature, and optical depth (see Appendix § \lx@sectionsign VII.3 ). This is true even in the absence of plausible biases coming from the observational constraints. Therefore, dust sizes may not necessarily trace the entire cold molecular gas disk; instead, they may represent a relatively compact region near the center, e.g., a bulge or a bar. James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observations of high- z unlensed DSFGs already confirm that their active star formation extends beyond the central bulges traced by dust [ 50 ] . Since dynamical masses ( M dyn ∝ radius M_{\rm dyn}\propto{\rm radius} ; see § \lx@sectionsign IV.1 and § \lx@sectionsign IV.2 ), adopting dust continuum sizes may therefore yield systematically lower dynamical masses than would be inferred using the full CO(1--0) extent. 5 5 5 We emphasize here that although CO(1–0) is generally optically thick and therefore does not linearly trace molecular column density, its luminosity remains correlated with molecular gas mass via α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} because, in the galaxy-scale observations, the velocity-integrated emission from ensembles of turbulent, self-gravitating molecular clouds scales approximately with the total molecular mass [ 26 , 91 , 8 , e.g.,] .

sections.heading: III.2 Molecular Gas Masses
sections.text: A value of α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} = 0.8 M ⊙ ​ ( K ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ pc 2 ) − 1 \rm M_{\odot}~{(K~km~{s}^{-1}~{pc}^{2})}^{-1} (units omitted hereafter) in Eqn. 1 is frequently assumed for high- z DSFGs, following studies of local ULIRGs [ 27 ] . This choice is largely motivated by dynamical mass arguments, as larger conversion factors would often imply molecular gas masses exceeding the available dynamical mass budget. With a dataset of galaxies that does not require corrections for either gravitational lensing or CO excitation, our aim here is to derive molecular gas masses using two complementary methods, which can then be compared with dynamical mass estimates. First, in § \lx@sectionsign III.2.1 , we fit the far-infrared-to-millimeter dust continuum with a general modified blackbody (GMBB; Eqn. 3 ) model, using the resolved dust size ( R dust R_{\rm dust} ) to constrain the dust surface density and optical depth, thereby reducing the otherwise strong degeneracy between T dust T_{\rm dust} , τ ν \tau_{\nu} , and M dust M_{\rm dust} . The resulting dust masses are converted to gas masses assuming a solar-metallicity gas-to-dust ratio of G/D = 100 [ 67 , 30 , 44 , e.g.,] . Second, we use the TUNER large velocity gradient (LVG) radiative transfer framework [ 10 ] to jointly model the CO line and dust continuum SEDs within a turbulent, multi-density interstellar medium or ISM ( § \lx@sectionsign III.2.2 ). In this approach, the molecular gas mass is constrained primarily by CO excitation and radiative transfer, while the dust emission is modeled self-consistently using the full GMBB method. Unlike the dust-only method, TUNER treats the characteristic emitting radius as a free parameter and therefore does not require the resolved dust size to define the emitting area. Both approaches are thus complementary, drawing on different observables and subject to different dominant uncertainties: one is driven primarily by the continuum SED and resolved dust geometry, while the other is constrained by the combined dust and CO excitation properties on galaxy-integrated scales. However, they are not fully independent, as both adopt the same dust opacity normalization ( κ ν \kappa_{\nu} ) and G/D = 100 and rely on simplified global descriptions of the dust emission. Consequently, differences in the inferred gas masses (Tables 3 and 6 ) primarily reflect the distinct constraints on dust temperature, β dust \beta_{\rm dust} , optical depth, and effective emitting size arising from continuum-only versus joint dust-and-gas radiative transfer modeling. To compare these gas-mass estimators, we further restrict our analysis to a subset of V z -GAL systems for which reliable LVG radiative transfer modeling can be carefully performed. From 21 DSFGs, we exclude sources containing multiple DSFGs that were blended within the Herschel/SPIRE beam but resolved in subsequent VLA V z -GAL and ALMA observations (e.g., HeLMS-47N and HeLMS-47S, HerBS-162SW and HerBS-162NE). For these systems, the peak of the far-infrared dust SED is poorly constrained because the Herschel photometry blends emission from multiple components. Three systems (HerBS-43a, HerBS-43b, and HerBS-70E), however, are retained because their robustly de-blended dust continuum flux densities are available from Stanley et al. [93] . After applying these selection criteria, the final sample comprises 12 galaxies with sufficiently well-constrained photometric and spectroscopic data to enable robust TUNER LVG modeling and a meaningful comparison with the other gas-mass estimation method. These 12 systems comprise two distinct subsets (Table 2 , Group-1 and Group-2). The first consists of seven sources whose CO(1–0) line profiles appear more consistent with a single Gaussian with a FWHM < 700 <700 km s -1 : HeLMS-39, HeLMS-54, HerS-8, HerBS-51, HerBS-70E, HerBS-165, and HerBS-169. The second includes five sources whose broad or complex CO(1–0) line profiles (FWHM ≳ 700 \gtrsim 700 km s -1 , see also § \lx@sectionsign II.3 ): HeLMS-50, HerBS-43a, HerBS-43b, HerBS-188, and HerBS-191. Hereafter, we refer to these two subsets as Group-1 and Group-2, respectively. Integrated dust continuum SED data points used in the following two sections are adopted from the z -GAL studies Neri et al. [72] and Ismail et al. [54] , including all the > 2 ​ σ >2\sigma detections. These have been restricted within the rest-frame 50 − 1000 ​ μ 50-1000~\mu m frequency range to cover the far-infrared dust continuum.

sections.heading: III.2.1 Gas Masses Derived using Dust Continuum and Galactic Gas-to-Dust Mass Ratio
III.2.2 Gas Masses from TUNER LVG Modeling
III.2.3 Comparison of Gas Mass Estimates
sections.text: Our targets have median CO(1–0) line luminosities of (0.89 ± \pm 0.11) × 10 11 \rm\times{10}^{11} and (0.94 ± \pm 0.50) × 10 11 ​ K ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ pc 2 \rm\times{10}^{11}K~km~{s}^{-1}~{pc}^{2} observed for Group-1 and Group-2 DSFGs, respectively. Under the traditional bimodal framework, α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} = 0.8 is commonly adopted for local ULIRGs and high- z DSFGs, SMGs, and quasars [ 27 , 16 , 8 , e.g.,] , whereas α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} = 4.3 --- comparable to the Milky Way value 10 10 10 also with Helium contribution — is typically assumed for local star-forming main-sequence galaxies. Applying α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} = 0.8 to our sample yields median molecular gas masses of 0.7 × 10 11 0.7\times{10}^{11} M ⊙ {\rm M}_{\odot} and 0.8 × 10 11 0.8\times{10}^{11} M ⊙ {\rm M}_{\odot} for Groups-1 and -2, respectively. In contrast, adopting α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} = 4.3 increases these estimates by a factor of ∼ 5 \sim 5 , giving median gas masses of 3.8 × 10 11 3.8\times{10}^{11} M ⊙ {\rm M}_{\odot} and 4.0 × 10 11 4.0\times{10}^{11} M ⊙ {\rm M}_{\odot} . Independently, the two gas-mass estimation methods described in § \lx@sectionsign III.2.1 and § \lx@sectionsign III.2.2 produce mutually consistent results for each source, except HerBS-43a, within their uncertainties. With the dust continuum-based method, we find median gas masses of (3.24 ± \pm 0.15) × 10 11 \times{10}^{11} M ⊙ {\rm M}_{\odot} and (3.98 ± \pm 0.59) × 10 11 \times{10}^{11} M ⊙ {\rm M}_{\odot} for Groups-1 and -2, respectively. These are broadly in agreement with those derived using the TUNER LVG method: (3.01 ± \pm 0.99) × 10 11 \times{10}^{11} M ⊙ {\rm M}_{\odot} and (5.18 ± \pm 0.42) × 10 11 \times{10}^{11} M ⊙ {\rm M}_{\odot} for Group-1 and Group-2. Results from the dust continuum-based method have only 2/12 DSFGs with inferred α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} values below 2, namely HeLMS-39 ( α CO , G / D = 1.85 − 0.23 + 0.31 \alpha_{\rm CO,G/D}={1.85}^{+0.31}_{-0.23} ) and HerS-8 ( α CO , G / D = 1.45 − 0.21 + 0.29 \alpha_{\rm CO,G/D}={1.45}^{+0.29}_{-0.21} ) from Group-1. In this method, we do not find any object with α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} ∼ \sim 0.8, which is typically assumed in the literature for local ULIRGs and high- z SMGs/DSFGs. Similarly, none of the galaxies in Groups-1 and -2 show α CO , LVG ≲ 2 \alpha_{\rm CO,LVG}\lesssim 2 using the TUNER, suggesting that the latest LVG model does not support α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} ∼ \sim 0.8 on galaxy-integrated scales for our sample of high- z DSFGs 11 11 11 Similar trend has also been seen for high- z dust-obscured galaxies [ 47 , e.g., W2246-0526;] and quasars (e.g., Cloverleaf; Prajapati et al., in prep.). , unlike the inference derived for local ULIRGs by Downes and Solomon [27] . Our derived gas masses in § \lx@sectionsign III.2.1 and III.2.2 are broadly consistent with each other. The median values lie significantly closer to those inferred using α CO = 4.3 \alpha_{\rm CO}=4.3 than to those obtained with α CO = 0.8 \alpha_{\rm CO}=0.8 , while the overall spread in α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} ( ∼ \sim 1.5–11.5) is similarly recovered across both approaches. Together, these results statistically favor a Milky Way-like CO–H 2 conversion factor for the DSFG sample in this work. Understanding such higher than α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} = 0.8 values in the context of the TUNER LVG radiative transfer model with CO excitation is important. Papadopoulos et al. [74] analyzed a large sample of luminous infrared galaxies (LIRGs) and found that single-phase radiative transfer models reproduce the low- J CO emission with a typical α CO ∼ 0.6 \alpha_{\rm CO}\sim 0.6 , consistent with the canonical ULIRG value. They argued that the low α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} is driven primarily by high gas velocity dispersion, with gas temperature playing a secondary role. However, they proposed that a cold, dense, gravitationally-bound gas phase, traced by high- J CO and dense-gas tracers (e.g., HCN, HCO + ), could contain a substantial fraction of the molecular mass and may increase α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} to 2–6. This highlighted the possibility that unresolved starbursts contain multiple gas density components, making a single global α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} an oversimplification. The TUNER modeling used in our work accounts for such a turbulent gas density distribution (see Figure 7 ). The lower-left and lower-center panels of Figure 7 for HerBS-51 show that although no single CO transition or dust continuum measurement can recover the full molecular gas reservoir in high- z DSFGs, the gas mass distribution indeed peaks around densities that are better probed by mid- J CO transitions ( J ∼ 4 − 7 J\sim 4-7 ) than by low- J CO lines. This is also in agreement with their CO level population showing an extended tail towards mid/high- J rotational levels (Figure 7 lower-right panel). 12 12 12 Such shifts toward higher rotational states are expected in high- z DSFGs owing to their elevated gas excitation and, potentially, the influence of increasing CMB temperature with redshift [ 47 , 76 , 18 , see] . In Appendix VII.5 , the remaining 11 DSFGs from our sample also show a similar trend. This highlights that CO(1–0) and other low- J lines are useful for tracing more diffuse ISM, while dense gas tracers remain important for revealing a significant fraction of the total gas mass in such high- z objects with high star formation rates. Most of our targets have at least 3 CO lines observed up to mid- J levels (see Table 4 ), showing consistency between observed and modeled CO luminosities. In the future, observing galaxy-integrated J > 6 J>6 CO transitions for our sample will be of further use to test the presented TUNER results. This is a limitation based on the currently available data, which will be addressed in future work.

sections.heading: IV Dynamical Tests of the Molecular Gas-Mass Estimates
sections.text: CO(1–0) emission is easily excited across a broad range of physical conditions, from cold and diffuse molecular gas to warmer and denser regions, making it the best-calibrated tracer of the total molecular gas reservoir in the local universe [ 85 , e.g.,] . For this reason, CO(1–0) is commonly used in integrated dynamical mass estimates, as both its linewidth and spatial extent are expected to trace the bulk of the gravitationally bound molecular medium. In contrast, higher- J J CO transitions and dust continuum emission preferentially probe warmer and denser gas and might appear more compact in DSFGs [ 14 , 10 ] . As a result, these tracers may not fully sample the system’s spatial extent, potentially biasing dynamical mass estimates. The CO(1–0) linewidth and radius, therefore, may provide a more representative characterization of the galaxy-scale gas dynamics via dynamical mass ( M dyn M_{\rm dyn} ) calculations. Central to the “ α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} tension” is a discrepancy between dynamical masses and molecular gas masses. In this section, we examine whether or not the molecular gas masses inferred in § \lx@sectionsign III.2 are consistent with the available dynamical mass budget — inferred from global CO(1–0) line properties — in high- z DSFGs. Specifically, we test whether the condition M gas ≤ M dyn M_{\rm gas}\leq M_{\rm dyn} is satisfied, as expected for systems that are gravitationally bound. 13 13 13 We use the inequality sign to reflect the lack of independent constraints on stellar masses and dark matter contributions in our dust-obscured, high- z sources. In this comparison, we use only the molecular gas and dynamical masses and assume the dust mass contribution is negligible.

sections.heading: IV.1 Dynamical Masses from the Isotropic Virial Estimator
sections.text: Assuming the cold molecular gas is gravitationally supported, a first-order consistency check on the gas masses can be obtained using an isotropic virial estimator for the dynamical mass (Eqn. 7 ). This approach assumes a spherically symmetric gas distribution and characterizes the kinematics via a one-dimensional velocity dispersion, σ 0 = FWHM / 2.35 \sigma_{0}={\rm FWHM}/2.35 [ 98 , 35 , 12 , e.g.,] 14 14 14 We note that because of the unresolved CO(1–0) FWHM used here for demonstrating a single pressure-support term, we cannot distinguish between the individual contributions from rotation, turbulence, mergers/accretion/outflows, and plausible beam-smeared velocity gradients. On the other hand, HerBS-43b from Group-2 also shows higher gas masses when compared to M dyn , vir M_{\rm dyn,vir} using LVG sizes, which can be attributed to its smaller LVG-derived size than the observed dust radius. Given that the presented LVG modeling is physically motivated, which will have improvements when new data of mid/high- J CO transitions and far-infrared continuum are added, we argue that the LVG-based gas masses ( M gas , LVG M_{\rm gas,LVG} ) — mutually consistent with dust continuum-derived gas masses ( M gas , G / D M_{\rm gas,G/D} ) — are overall consistent with the dynamical masses of the sources as expected from a simple isotropic virial estimator. In summary, Figure 8 shows that the gas masses derived using both methods-1 and -2 can be reconciled with the dynamical mass constraints once realistic estimates of the cold molecular gas extent are adopted. Our TUNER modeling further reveals substantial source-to-source variation in the inferred gas masses, reflecting a variety in intrinsic ISM conditions and the galaxies’ excitation properties. This is evident from the considerably larger spread in the LVG-based gas masses relative to those obtained from method-1. Together, these results argue against the assumption of a universal CO-to-H 2 conversion factor on galaxy-integrated scales for our sample of high- z DSFGs. Instead, the appropriate value of α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} appears to vary from system to system according to the physical state and excitation conditions of the molecular gas. Consequently, our analysis does not require adoption of the canonical ULIRG value of α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} = 0.8 to reconcile the inferred gas masses with the available dynamical mass constraints (see also § \lx@sectionsign III.2.3 ), highlighting the dynamical viability of intermediate (e.g., α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} = 2–3) or near-Galactic conversion factors. Moreover, if applied indiscriminately, α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} = 0.8 may systematically underestimate the molecular gas content of many high- z dusty galaxies – see also a recent theoretical work by Anirudh et al. [1] . We therefore suggest constraining α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} on a source-by-source basis wherever possible, using detailed radiative-transfer modeling in combination with complementary observational/dynamical diagnostics.

sections.heading: IV.2 Dynamical Masses from Rotation and Pressure Support
sections.text: When the underlying geometry and kinematics of a galaxy are unknown, the isotropic virial estimator provides a useful first-order approach for assessing the dynamical masses of unresolved systems. This is particularly relevant for many dusty galaxies in the early universe, whose dynamical structures are often poorly constrained. However, the isotropic virial estimator effectively averages over the source geometry and folds together the contributions of ordered rotation, turbulence, accretion, and other dynamical processes into the observed CO(1–0) linewidths. With time, the growing capabilities of modern radio and submillimeter interferometers, including ALMA, NOEMA, and the VLA, have enabled an increasing number of high- z systems to be spatially resolved. These studies reveal a diverse range of dynamical states and corresponding geometries. Some of the most luminous dusty galaxies appear to be associated with major merger events [ 98 , 79 , e.g.,] . In contrast, several others, including both gravitationally lensed and unlensed sources, show ordered rotation indicative of cold molecular gas disks [ 95 , 14 , 89 , e.g.,] . The distinction, however, is not always clear, except in cases of ongoing mergers where multiple components are both spatially and kinematically distinct and not aligned along the same line of sight. High- z DSFGs, therefore, appear to comprise a heterogeneous population, spanning coalescing systems, late-stage mergers transitioning toward more disk-like configurations, and galaxies with well-ordered rotating disks. For example, GN20 ( z ∼ 4.1 z\sim 4.1 ) exhibits a regularly rotating CO(2–1) disk [ 49 ] , although [ 10 ] suggest it may have experienced an interaction in the recent past. 16 16 16 This diversity also raises the possibility that dynamically disturbed systems in the early universe can settle into disk-like configurations on relatively short timescales. Therefore, in this section, we propose to use a “mixed estimator” of dynamical masses for high- z dusty galaxies (Eqn. 8 ). This approach is consistent with the studies of star-forming main-sequence disks and starburst galaxies up to z ∼ 4 z\sim 4 [ 40 , 35 , 81 , e.g.,] using various components of the ISM 17 17 17 These studies span from stellar and ionized gas tracers to cold gas resolved data using [CI], [CII], and mid- J CO transitions [ 82 , see also] . , which often model the resolved kinematics with both rotational and velocity-dispersion contribution. We therefore compare the mixed estimator (Eqn. 8 ) to the isotropic virial estimator for a representative range of observed properties. Assuming identical sizes, a median velocity dispersion of ∼ 34 \sim 34 km s -1 (Table 2 ), and characteristic CO(1–0) linewidths of ∼ 500 \sim 500 km s -1 (Group-1) and ∼ 1000 \sim 1000 km s -1 (Group-2), we find that matching the dynamical masses derived from the mixed and isotropic virial estimators requires inclination angles of only ∼ 26 ∘ \sim 26^{\circ} – 28 ∘ 28^{\circ} . 19 19 19 Similarly, approaches discussed by Bothwell et al. [12] , namely virial and rotating disk estimators, also require an inclination of ∼ 22 ∘ \sim 22^{\circ} to be mutually compared. Varying the pressure-support coefficient over the range k = 1 k=1 –10 yields a similar result, with only a weak dependence on the adopted linewidth. Such systematically low inclination angles are unlikely to be ubiquitous among DSFGs, suggesting that generic assumptions may not adequately capture the diversity of their underlying dynamical structures. This outcome highlights a key limitation of applying Eqn. 8 to unresolved observations, despite its greater flexibility in accounting for turbulent and dispersion-supported gas motions compared to a pure rotational disk estimator. The observed CO FWHM reflects a combination of ordered rotation, random motions, and potentially other sources of kinematic broadening, whereas unresolved data for most high- z DSFGs do not allow these contributions to be disentangled. Consequently, the same integrated linewidth can arise from different combinations of v rot v_{\rm rot} and σ 0 \sigma_{0} , leading to substantially different inferred dynamical masses. In addition, DSFGs are not spherically symmetric; the observed linewidth therefore depends on viewing angle, such that galaxies with identical intrinsic kinematics but different inclinations can exhibit different FWHM values. 20 20 20 Additional velocity components, such as inflows, outflows, or merger-induced motions, may further contribute to the observed linewidth. The requirement for nearly face-on inclinations when equating the two estimators thus reflects the fundamentally different assumptions underlying an arguably more physically motivated pressure-supported rotating disk geometry and a spherically symmetric virialized system. The latter does not account for geometric and inclination-dependent effects that are explicitly relevant in disk-like systems. As a result, unresolved CO linewidth measurements alone do not provide sufficient information to uniquely constrain both the rotational velocity ( v rot v_{\rm rot} ) and intrinsic velocity dispersion ( σ 0 \sigma_{0} ). We therefore rely on the apparent consistency between gas and dynamical masses inferred from the isotropic virial estimator, given that it remains the most practical first-order method for unresolved DSFG populations. Nonetheless, we argue that the mixed estimator (Eqn. 8 ) is likely to provide a more realistic representation of DSFG dynamics once independent constraints on the underlying geometry and kinematics are obtained from resolved observations and detailed dynamical modeling [ 13 , 25 , 65 , e.g., with GalPaK 3D , 3D BAROLO, DysmalPy 3D ;] .

sections.heading: IV.3 GN20, an Archetype Dusty Galaxy
sections.text: GN20, at a redshift of z = 4.055 z=4.055 , is an unlensed dusty galaxy in the GOODS-North field. Its integrated CO emission was first reported by [ 15 ] , while subsequent CO(2–1) observations spatially resolved its cold molecular gas disk (size: 7 ± 2 7\pm 2 kpc) and kinematics [ 49 ] . Resolved dust continuum imaging later revealed a dust-emitting radius of R dust ∼ 5.3 R_{\rm dust}\sim 5.3 kpc at 880 ​ μ 880~\mu m [ 51 ] . As one of the very few unlensed high- z SMGs with spatially resolved CO(2–1) kinematics — the lowest- J CO transition resolved in such a system — GN20 provides a unique benchmark for testing how dynamical masses inferred from unresolved CO linewidths compare with those derived from resolved observations. We therefore use GN20 as a case study to investigate the impact of assumptions underlying the use of galaxy-integrated data in the proposed dynamical mass estimator (Eqn. 8 ). We first investigate the conventional isotropic virial estimator (Eqn. 7 ) for GN20, using the integrated CO(2–1) linewidth ( 730 ± 140 730\pm 140 km s − 1 {\rm s}^{-1} ) and compare the resulting dynamical masses with the TUNER LVG-derived gas mass 21 21 21 Assuming that the self-consistent TUNER LVG modeling provides the most robust molecular gas mass estimates of GN20 currently available. from Boogaard et al. 10 (Figure 8 ). sections.heading: V.1 Integrated molecular gas masses and α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} of dusty star-forming systems across cosmic time
sections.text: There has been considerable debate regarding whether or not the α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} conversion factor is bimodal across galaxy populations [e.g., 24 , 41 , 86 , 29 , 5 , and references therein] . Under the traditional bimodal framework, α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} = 0.8 is commonly adopted for local ULIRGs and high- z DSFGs, SMGs, and quasars [ 27 , 16 , 8 , 107 , e.g.,] , whereas a value of Galactic α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} = 4.3 is typically assumed for local star-forming main-sequence galaxies. Theoretical studies have long discussed that α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} is not adequately described by bimodality, but instead it varies continuously with the physical conditions of the ISM [ 71 , 70 ] . Although many observational studies have discussed this, [ 48 ] and [ 76 ] attempt to quantify the trend better using larger sample sizes. However, unresolved dust and gas observations provide only limited constraints on the internal ISM properties of high- z galaxies; methods such as the TUNER LVG radiative transfer modeling explored in our work offer a valuable means to infer these properties. The commonly adopted α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} of 0.8 for local ULIRGs (with a reported range spanning 0.3–1.3) originated from the study by [ 27 ] , which was subsequently adopted for high- z DSFGs, SMGs, and quasars. This conversion factor gained widespread acceptance because it yielded molecular gas masses broadly consistent with the available dynamical mass estimates. In that work, α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} was derived using radiative transfer modeling; however, the analysis was limited primarily to observations of the CO(1–0) and CO(2–1) transitions. Based on these data, the authors inferred relatively low gas densities, a condition that leads to a low α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} , as α CO ∝ n H 2 / T b \alpha_{\rm CO}\propto\sqrt{n_{\rm H_{2}}}\,/\,{T_{\rm b}} [ 92 ] . However, observations of higher- J CO transitions, particularly after the Herschel era, have revealed that local ULIRGs are generally highly excited systems [ 62 , 83 , see e.g.,] . Modern radiative transfer analyses of these sources (Weiss et al., in prep.) no longer support the low gas densities inferred from the limited low- J datasets available to [ 27 ] . Consequently, the latest LVG and other excitation models often favor substantially higher α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} values – see also the discussion by Papadopoulos et al. [74] for LIRGs. Additionally, a recent theoretical study of massive star-forming galaxies (on and above the main sequence) at cosmic noon by Anirudh et al. [1] also suggests that the α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} is ∼ 1 − 5 \sim 1-5 in the central regions of their massive simulated galaxies, but these values rise sharply beyond the central few kiloparsecs. Leading to a range in α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} of about 1.5–8.5 for our sample, the dust SED-based method-1 ( § \lx@sectionsign III.2.1 ) support this interpretation, for which the inferred large gas masses are consistent, within the uncertainties, with those derived from the detailed radiative transfer modeling performed with TUNER ( α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} = 2.6–11.5, method-2; § \lx@sectionsign III.2.2 ). In particular, TUNER simultaneously models the integrated dust and CO SEDs, providing a self-consistent framework for constraining the gas excitation conditions and molecular gas content of these sources. It is important, however, to note the current limitations of the TUNER LVG modeling. It relies on the currently available galaxy-integrated measurements, which are robustly anchored using CO(1–0) but lack constraints on CO transitions above J = 6 J=6 for all of our targets. Consequently, the inferred physical conditions can be refined with improved measurements, providing stronger constraints on the warmer and denser molecular gas components. It will also enable a more robust characterization of the range of gas excitation conditions present in these systems. The tension between gas-based and dynamical estimates of α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} is also not unique to CO or dust as molecular gas tracers. Similar discrepancies have been reported using alternative probes such as [CI] and [CII], when their Galactic calibrations are adopted [ 31 ] . More broadly, studies of dust-obscured star-forming galaxies across cosmic time consistently find that molecular gas masses inferred from ISM tracers exceed those implied by unresolved dynamical analyses [ 108 , 31 , 46 , 32 , e.g.,] , leading to the requirement for their lower α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} conversion factors. While [ 32 ] propose metallicity evolution as one of the plausible explanations, this is unlikely to dominate in the most luminous high- z z DSFGs, which are expected to have near-solar or super-solar metallicities [ 29 , 44 ] .

sections.heading: V.2 Are large molecular gas masses and Galactic α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} values dynamically allowed?
sections.text: The CO(1–0) line luminosities of our high- z z V z -GAL DSFGs are consistent with those of the broader DSFG population [ 76 , see Figure 2 of] , indicating that these galaxies are representative rather than exceptional systems. Their gas-mass estimates based on the dust SED and the TUNER LVG analysis ( § \lx@sectionsign III.2.1 and § \lx@sectionsign III.2.2 ) consistently imply large molecular gas reservoirs, encompassing near-Galactic conversion factors within the inferred broad range of α CO ∼ 1.5 − 11.5 \alpha_{\rm CO}\sim 1.5-11.5 . The central question is, therefore, whether such large gas masses are compatible with the observed dynamics, or whether the kinematics instead necessarily require the commonly adopted ULIRG value of α CO = 0.8 \alpha_{\rm CO}=0.8 . When our proposed rotating thick-disk “mixed estimator” (Eqn. 8 , Figure 9 ) is combined with compact dust radii, the inferred dynamical masses are relatively small, particularly for Group-1, yielding upper limits that can fall below the gas-based estimates. However, using GN20 as a case study, we argue that these constraints would relax substantially once more realistic cold gas extents and geometry are adopted. Assuming a smoothly distributed cold gas component, the TUNER LVG-inferred sizes are expected to be broadly consistent with the radii inferred from resolved low- J CO emission extents (e.g., GN20). The isotropic virial estimator (Eqn. 7 , Figure 8 ) provides a complementary test by avoiding explicit assumptions about disk inclination and rotational support. Using the LVG-derived gas radii in the virial estimator, the median dynamical limits increase to α CO , dyn , vir ≤ 4.46 ± 1.10 \alpha_{\rm CO,dyn,vir}\leq 4.46\pm 1.10 for Group-1 and ≤ 10.64 ± 3.86 \leq 10.64\pm 3.86 for Group-2, fully encompassing the values inferred from both gas-mass methods. The particularly large dynamical limits obtained for Group-2 should nevertheless be interpreted as conservative upper bounds. Because both dynamical estimators scale approximately with the square of the observed CO linewidth, galaxies with broad integrated profiles naturally yield much larger dynamical masses. As discussed in § \lx@sectionsign IV.2 for unresolved systems, broad linewidths may contain a combination of ordered rotation, turbulence, mergers, or projection effects. Consequently, the Group-2 limits should be used with caution (see also Appendix § \lx@sectionsign VII.2 ). Overall, the comparison in Table 8 , supported by Figures 8 and 9 , demonstrates that the inferred high α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} values cannot be completely ruled out by the available dynamical constraints. Instead, the apparent preference for α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} = 0.8 may arise mainly when compact effective sizes and inclination-dependent rotating-disk models are applied to unresolved observations. Once plausible uncertainties in the cold gas extent, geometry, and kinematic structure are taken into account, intermediate (e.g., α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} = 2–3) or near-Galactic α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} values remain dynamically viable across our sample (e.g., GN20, § \lx@sectionsign IV.3 ). We therefore find no dynamical justification for universally adopting α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} = 0.8 in the presented high- z DSFGs here. To avoid underestimating molecular gas masses systematically, α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} = 0.8 should not be assumed for DSFGs unless supported by ISM and/or dynamical modeling. Rather, the appropriate conversion factor is likely to vary from source to source. Robust estimates would require combining independent gas-mass tracers, resolved gas and dust distributions, and supporting dynamical models [ 13 , e.g., GalPaK 3D ;] that overcome the limitations set by unresolved observations.

sections.heading: V.3 Why do rotating thick-disk-based dynamical masses remain low?
sections.text: The dependence of the inferred α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} limits on the adopted dynamical estimator naturally raises the question of why the rotating thick-disk prescription — although generic and flexible for accommodating various v rot v_{\rm rot} / σ 0 \sigma_{0} values — systematically yields lower masses than the spherically symmetric virial estimator. We argue that this primarily reflects the application of a geometrically specific model to unresolved observations, where several key quantities cannot be directly constrained. • Cold gas extents: Both dynamical mass estimators scale linearly with the effective radius of the cold gas distribution, which remains uncertain. Our TUNER LVG radiative transfer analysis, together with resolved studies of DSFGs [ 14 , 10 , e.g.,] , indicates that molecular gas may significantly extend beyond the dust continuum. This suggests that dust-based sizes likely underestimate the true spatial extent over which the observed linewidths are produced. • Source geometry: While the isotropic virial estimator performs well for unresolved data — and, in our case, yields dynamical masses broadly encompassing the inferred gas masses — more sophisticated approaches require spatially and spectrally resolved observations. If DSFGs are assumed to be rotating thick disks, the poorly constrained inclination angles introduce substantial uncertainties in the derived dynamical masses. Moreover, the dust morphology may not accurately trace the more extended distribution of cold molecular gas in high- z DSFGs. Consequently, resolved cold gas observations are essential to fully characterize the source geometry and to assess its impact on dynamical mass estimates. • CO linewidth: The integrated FWHM of CO lines cannot be uniquely decomposed into ordered rotation and turbulent dispersive medium in unresolved galaxies. This is extremely relevant for bright dusty sources across redshifts, many of which are proposed to be involved in ongoing/past merger activities. Turbulence, mergers, beam smearing, cold mode accretion, outflows, and multiple unresolved components may all broaden the observed CO line profile. Consequently, the integrated FWHM used in any dynamical mass estimator introduces a fundamental degeneracy into geometry-dependent dynamical models. Ultimately, resolving these uncertainties requires spatially and spectrally resolved observations of the cold gas reservoir, particularly with low- J CO emissions, which directly traces the bulk molecular gas distribution and its kinematics in high- z DSFGs. Such observations are essential for constraining the gas extent, source geometry, and the relative contributions of ordered rotation and turbulent motions (i.e., v rot v_{\rm rot} / σ 0 \sigma_{0} ). While high-resolution dust continuum observations provide a more accessible and observationally efficient means of obtaining initial size estimates, they are unlikely to capture the full extent of the cold molecular gas reservoir and its dynamics. Resolved low- J CO observations with ALMA, NOEMA, and future facilities such as the ngVLA will therefore be essential. At the same time, resolved observations of alternative tracers, including [CII], [CI], and mid- J CO transitions, can provide complementary, intermediate constraints on galaxy kinematics; e.g., the recent NOEMA 3D survey for high- z main-sequence galaxies by [ 20 , 57 ] , and several [CII] studies [ 68 , 84 , e.g.,] . Together, these data will enable more physically motivated dynamical mass estimates and, consequently, more robust upper limits on α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} than those obtained under the isotropic virial assumption.

sections.heading: V.4 Group-1 versus Group-2 DSFGs: Different kinematic classes?
sections.text: The distinction between Group-1 and Group-2 sources suggests that the V z -GAL DSFG population is unlikely to be kinematically uniform. Group-1 galaxies, characterized by comparatively simple CO(1–0) line profiles, occupy a relatively homogeneous region of parameter space in which the unresolved kinematics can be reproduced by similar combinations of inclination and dynamical support. In contrast, Group-2 galaxies exhibit broader and/or more complex CO(1–0) profiles and span a substantially wider range of acceptable dynamical solutions. Their larger integrated linewidths and, in some cases, larger dust sizes naturally yield higher dynamical masses and consequently weaker upper limits on α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} . This broader distribution may reflect greater diversity in the underlying gas dynamics, arising from enhanced turbulence, non-circular motions, mergers, or multiple unresolved kinematic components. For example, GN20 — with plausible recent interaction [ 21 , 102 , 10 ] — occupies a similar region of parameter space to the Group-2 sources in Figures 8 and 9 . Although we note that marginal differences in the viewing angle of the system’s geometry can change the FWHM shapes, large differences in linewidths are more likely to arise because of dynamics. We therefore interpret the two groups as representing different degrees of dynamical complexity rather than a strict disk–merger division. While the available unresolved observations do not uniquely distinguish between the physical mechanisms responsible for the observed linewidths, they suggest that our high- z DSFGs likely span a continuum of dynamical states, with Group-1 representing the more homogeneous end of the distribution and Group-2 encompassing systems with increasingly diverse kinematic configurations. This interpretation is broadly consistent with recent theoretical studies, which suggest that unresolved kinematic measurements may not fully capture the dynamical complexity of massive high- z star-forming galaxies. Cosmological simulations indicate that the molecular gas is preferentially confined to the rotating disk, with expected v rot / σ 0 v_{\rm rot}/\sigma_{0} ratios approximately 2–3 times higher than those of the HI component [ 60 ] . Furthermore, FIRE-2 simulations show that the mid-plane pressure is well described by the weight of the gas disk and scales approximately linearly with the star formation rate surface density, a quantity that can be inferred from resolved dust continuum observations [ 45 ] . Consistent with this picture, simulation-based studies of z ≳ 1 z\gtrsim 1 galaxies with stellar masses M ∗ > 10 11 ​ M ⊙ M_{\ast}>{10}^{11}~{\rm M}_{\odot} find that dynamical masses can be underestimated by up to 40% if turbulent pressure gradients are neglected in disk models [ 105 ] . Together, these results provide theoretical motivation for modeling DSFGs as rotating, pressure-supported systems while highlighting the importance of spatially resolved gas and dust observations for disentangling rotational support, turbulence, and merger-driven motions, and for testing the validity of such dynamical models. Due to their plausibly complex gas dynamics, DSFGs are expected to host high gas fractions, intense star formation, and elevated star-formation rate surface densities ( Σ SFR \Sigma_{\rm SFR} ). Figure 12 compares the observed and LVG-inferred Σ SFR \Sigma_{\rm SFR} values and explores their relation to source size and gas excitation. The LVG-inferred results reveal a clear correlation between Σ SFR \Sigma_{\rm SFR} and molecular gas excitation, with more compact galaxies exhibiting higher Σ SFR \Sigma_{\rm SFR} and stronger high- J J ( J > 6 J>6 ) CO emission. While this trend is physically expected, it is much weaker when the observed dust continuum sizes are adopted, supporting the argument from § \lx@sectionsign III.1.2 that optical depth effects cause dust emission to underestimate the true extent of the ISM. We find a similar trend if we replace the Σ SFR \Sigma_{\rm SFR} with the LVG-inferred molecular gas surface density, consistent with dense/warm ISM leading to higher- J CO excitation. In contrast, we find no correlation between the α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} conversion factor and either Σ SFR \Sigma_{\rm SFR} or source size (Figure 12 , right panel). Using the observed dust sizes, Σ SFR \Sigma_{\rm SFR} ranges from 20–400 M ⊙ \rm{M}_{\odot} yr -1 kpc -2 , with the most compact systems approaching the “maximum starburst” regime. Adopting the larger ISM sizes inferred from the TUNER LVG analysis lowers this range to 0.5–200 M ⊙ \rm{M}_{\odot} yr -1 kpc -2 , although these galaxies remain capable of sustaining highly turbulent and intermittent ISM conditions, potentially shaped by processes such as cold gas inflows, merging gas streams, past/ongoing galaxy interactions, and feedback-driven strong winds. Resolving the physical origin of the diversity between Group-1 and Group-2 systems, therefore, requires spatially resolved CO imaging. Such observations will constrain the spatial extent of the cold molecular gas and provide robust measurements of disk inclination, dynamical mass, and the relative contributions of rotational support, and turbulence in high- z DSFG populations. At the same time, galaxy-integrated CO SLEDs anchored by at least CO(1–0) or CO(2–1), together with dust continuum and mid/high- J CO observations, will remain essential for jointly constraining molecular gas masses and calibrating the characteristic spatial scales of these galaxies through semi-empirical approaches such as TUNER. Altogether, these complementary resolved and integrated observations will help reduce the current uncertainties in α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} and determine whether Group-1 and Group-2 sources in our sample reflect differences in their dynamical states, evolutionary stages, or both.

sections.heading: V.5 α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} and distance from the star-forming main-sequence
sections.text: Given the heavily dust-obscured nature of high- z DSFGs, one of the main challenges is obtaining reliable stellar mass ( M ∗ M_{\ast} ) estimates, which are required to determine their location relative to the SFR– M ∗ M_{\ast} main-sequence. Accurate stellar masses are also essential for estimating gas fractions and for deriving α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} upper bounds from dynamical masses after accounting for the stellar mass contribution (e.g., GN20 in Figure 9 ). Recent rest-frame near-infrared observations of 13 such unlensed dusty galaxies using the JWST [ 50 ] indicate high dust extinctions, which motivates expanding the observations up to mid-infrared to get robust stellar contributions. The observed high, total infrared luminosities in these sources are expected to obscure even strong nebular lines such as H ​ α \rm H{\alpha} [ 102 , see e.g., GN20;] and Pa ​ α \rm Pa{\alpha} [ 6 , e.g.,] , making the stellar mass and metallicity estimates of such systems extremely challenging. Such a scenario also cautions about using alternative, independent α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} estimation techniques such as stellar mass-metallicity relations [ 41 , e.g.,] . Even in local dusty merger systems, metallicity determinations remain subject to significant uncertainties arising from complex stellar populations, underlying Balmer absorption, merger-driven gas inflows, and spatial variations in chemical abundances. These challenges are likely to be even more severe at high redshift, where limited sensitivity and spatial resolution further complicate the interpretation of nebular emission-line diagnostics. Consequently, α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} estimates based on metallicity should be interpreted with caution and, whenever possible, cross-validated against independent constraints. In particular, at high redshift, such estimates should be compared with cold gas-based dynamical and semi-empirical (e.g., TUNER LVG) constraints. Although the efforts to characterize the dust extinction and eventually stellar masses and metallicity, via multiwavelength SED fitting tools, rest-frame optical/near-infrared, and mid-infrared data for larger samples of high- z DSFGs are currently in a nascent stage, facilities such as the JWST and ground-based ≳ \gtrsim 10m-class telescopes, alongside future missions (e.g., PRIMA), hold great potential to explore this parameter space to reveal the nature of the high- z dusty systems and their multi-phase ISM in the context of galaxy evolution over cosmic time.

sections.heading: VI Summary
sections.text: The CO–H 2 conversion factor ( α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} ) remains the most discussed source of uncertainty in determining molecular gas masses of high- z dusty star-forming galaxies (DSFGs). Using the largest to date homogeneous sample of 21 unlensed DSFGs at z = 1 − 4 z=1-4 with integrated CO(1–0) measurements and resolved ALMA 1 mm continuum imaging, we revisit the α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} discrepancy. Restricting our analysis to the 12 galaxies with the tighter modeling constraints, we estimate molecular gas masses independently using dust SED modeling ( § \lx@sectionsign III.2.1 ) and the TUNER multi-component LVG framework ( § \lx@sectionsign III.2.2 ). Although these approaches are not fully independent, as they share assumptions regarding the gas-to-dust ratio of 100 [ 67 , e.g.,] , dust opacity normalization [ 28 ] , and global dust modeling, they nevertheless yield consistent gas masses within their uncertainty. Together, they imply a wide range of α CO ∼ 1.5 − 11.5 \alpha_{\rm CO}\sim 1.5-11.5 (including Helium contribution) with median values of about 3.4 and 5.1, respectively, which are substantially larger than the commonly adopted α CO = 0.8 \alpha_{\rm CO}=0.8 for high- z DSFGs. In the context of α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} tension, we compare the resulting gas masses to dynamical constraints derived from both the isotropic “virial” estimator ( § \lx@sectionsign IV.1 ) and the proposed “mixed” dynamical mass estimator ( § \lx@sectionsign IV.2 ) that assumes DSFGs as rotating, pressure-supported thick disks. Our main findings are: 1. The isotropic virial estimator yields dynamical upper limits consistent with the independently derived gas masses once plausible cold-gas sizes are adopted (Figure 8 ), demonstrating that the available dynamical constraints do not strictly require α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} = 0.8. 2. In contrast, the unresolved “mixed” dynamical estimator systematically underestimates dynamical masses, producing artificially low α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} upper limits (Table 8 ). Using the archetype GN20 as a case study ( § \lx@sectionsign IV.3 ), we show that incorporating resolved gas geometry, inclination, and the partition between ordered rotation and turbulent dispersion recovers the missing dynamical mass using the proposed “mixed” estimator, bringing the dynamical constraints into agreement with the LVG-derived α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} [ 10 ] . 3. Under the adopted assumptions of a fixed gas-to-dust ratio (G/D = 100) and dust opacity normalization ( κ ν \kappa_{\nu} ; Table 6 ), the TUNER model constrains the CO abundance required to reproduce the observed CO SLEDs. These results, therefore, suggest that uncertainties in ISM modeling and dynamical mass estimates may contribute substantially to the apparent global α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} discrepancy. Leaving the G/D ratio free in TUNER requires 9/12 DSFGs to have a G/D ratio between 200 and 380, which appears unrealistic for such dusty sources [ 29 , 44 , see] . Therefore, TUNER results presented here do not directly constrain the gas metallicity under the G/D = 100 assumption. 4. TUNER modeling reveals a multi-phase molecular ISM in high- z DSFGs: low- J CO traces the most extended diffuse reservoir with LVG-inferred sizes ∼ 2 × \sim 2\times larger than the observed 1 mm dust (Figure 6 ), while higher- J CO lines probe compact, dense star-forming gas that contains a substantial fraction of the total molecular mass. This naturally explains the elevated α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} > > 0.8, consistent with expectations for local ULIRGs [ 74 ] . In summary, our analysis indicates that the available data do not require the commonly adopted α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} = 0.8 for high- z DSFGs. Instead, intermediate ( ∼ 2 − 3 \sim 2-3 ) to near-Galactic values remain dynamically viable once plausible cold molecular gas extents and geometric uncertainties are taken into account. The conclusion is conditional on the adopted assumptions regarding the gas-to-dust ratio, dust opacity, gas geometry, and unresolved kinematics, but demonstrates that current dynamical constraints do not uniquely favor a low conversion factor such as α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} = 0.8 in these systems. Robust calibration of α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} will require physically motivated molecular gas mass estimates from multi-component ISM models such as TUNER, together with resolved measurements of cold-gas geometry and kinematics. Improved constraints on dust properties and gas-to-dust ratio in high- z DSFGs will further complement these. While resolved CO(1–0) observations remain observationally demanding until the advent of the ngVLA, resolved studies of complementary tracers such as [CII], [CI], and J = 2 − 4 J=2-4 CO lines can provide valuable intermediate constraints on the gas dynamics and molecular gas distribution. Establishing such observational benchmarks will be essential for robustly calibrating the global α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} of massive galaxies in the early universe.

sections.text: For inclination defined in the usual sense ( 0 ≤ i ≤ π / 2 0\leq i\leq\pi/2 , with i = 0 i=0 for a face-on disk and i = π / 2 i=\pi/2 for an edge-on disk), the probability that a randomly oriented disk will be observed to have a given inclination will be p ⁡ ( i ) ​ d ​ i = sin ​ i ​ d ​ i p(i)\,di={\rm sin}\,i\,di . The result for p ⁡ ( i ) p(i) then follows from the symmetry between one galaxy observed by an ensemble of astronomers and one astronomer observing an ensemble of galaxies. p ⁡ ( i ) p(i) satisfies the normalization condition required of a probability distribution, namely that when integrated over the full range of values taken by i i , ∫ 0 π / 2 p ⁡ ( i ) ​ 𝑑 i = ∫ 0 π / 2 sin ​ i ​ 𝑑 i = 1 \int^{\pi/2}_{0}p(i)\,di=\int^{\pi/2}_{0}{\rm sin}\,i\,di=1 (13) As a consequence, for any function f ⁡ ( i ) f(i) with the property that f ⁡ ( i ) ​ sin ​ i f(i)\,{\rm sin}\,i is nowhere infinite over the interval [ 0 , π / 2 ] [0,\pi/2] , the mean value of f ⁡ ( i ) f(i) for a random distribution of inclinations will be ⟨ f ⁡ ( i ) ⟩ = ∫ 0 π / 2 f ⁡ ( i ) ​ sin ​ i ​ 𝑑 i \left<f(i)\right>=\int^{\pi/2}_{0}f(i)\,{\rm sin}\,i\,di (14) For the reader’s convenience, we review a few idealized examples that occur in the context of galaxy kinematics. In many situations, we are less interested in estimating ⟨ f ⁡ ( i ) ⟩ \left<f(i)\right> than in determining the form of the relationship y = f ⁡ ( i , x 1 , x 2 , … ) y=f(i,x_{1},x_{2},\dots) for an observed quantity y y that depends on inclination and (perhaps) a number of intrinsic galaxy parameters { x 1 , x 2 , … } \{x_{1},x_{2},\dots\} . In this context, it is convenient to exploit the availability of a statistical test — the Kolmogorov-Smirnov (K-S) test — for comparing theoretical and observed cumulative distribution functions (CDFs). For measured { Y 1 , Y 2 , … } \{Y_{1},Y_{2},\dots\} , the observed CDF( Y Y ) is defined as the fraction of the sample with Y i < Y Y_{i}<Y . If f ⁡ ( i , x 1 , x 2 , … ) f(i,x_{1},x_{2},\dots) is a monotonically increasing function of i i , the theoretical CDF( y y ) takes a particularly simple form: CDF ⁡ ( y ) = ∫ 0 i up p ⁡ ( i ) ​ 𝑑 i = ∫ 0 i up sin ​ i ​ 𝑑 i = 1 − cos ​ i up {\rm CDF}(y)=\int^{i_{\rm up}}_{0}p(i)\,di=\int^{i_{\rm up}}_{0}{\rm sin}\,i\,di=1-{\rm cos}\,i_{\rm up} (18) where the upper bound i up i_{\rm up} is implicitly defined by y = f ⁡ ( i up , x 1 , x 2 , … ) y=f(i_{\rm up},x_{1},x_{2},\dots) (19) Likewise, if f ⁡ ( i , x 1 , x 2 , … ) f(i,x_{1},x_{2},\dots) is a monotonically decreasing function of i i , we have CDF ⁡ ( y ) = ∫ i low π / 2 p ⁡ ( i ) ​ 𝑑 i = ∫ i low π / 2 sin ​ i ​ 𝑑 i = cos ​ i low {\rm CDF}(y)=\int^{\pi/2}_{i_{\rm low}}p(i)\,di=\int^{\pi/2}_{i_{\rm low}}{\rm sin}\,i\,di={\rm cos}\,i_{\rm low} (20) in terms of a lower bound i low i_{\rm low} implicitly defined by y = f ⁡ ( i low , x 1 , x 2 , … ) y=f(i_{\rm low},x_{1},x_{2},\dots) (21) Many problems of interest fall into one of these two simple categories; for example, if a galaxy’s observed line-of-sight velocity width Δ ​ v \Delta v is due to a combination of a velocity dispersion term v disp v_{\rm disp} and a rotation term v rot ​ sin ​ i v_{\rm rot}\,{\rm sin}\,i added in quadrature Δ ​ v ​ ( i , v disp , v rot ) ≈ ( v disp 2 + v rot 2 ​ sin 2 ​ i ) 1 2 \Delta v\,(i,v_{\rm disp},v_{\rm rot})\approx\Big(v_{\rm disp}^{2}+v_{\rm rot}^{2}\,{\rm sin}^{2}i\Big)^{\frac{1}{2}} (22) then as a function of i i , Δ ​ v \Delta v is monotonically increasing. Solving Equation 19 for i up i_{\rm up} then allows us to substitute into Equation 18 (as, in a different context, solving Equation 21 for i low i_{\rm low} would allow us to substitute into Equation 20 ). The resulting CDF( y y ) can then be compared to the observed CDF( Y Y ), for different choices of { x 1 , x 2 } = { v disp , v rot } \{x_{1},x_{2}\}=\{v_{\rm disp},v_{\rm rot}\} , using the K-S test. In the present paper, we are merely interested in whether the inclinations we have inferred for our DSFG sample are consistent with the expectations for a random distribution (i.e., there are no other relevant parameters { x 1 , x 2 , … } \{x_{1},x_{2},\dots\} ). Thus, f ⁡ ( i ) = i f(i)=i , which (trivially) increases monotonically with i i , and we can use Equation 18 to calculate a theoretical CDF( y y ). In Figure 15 , we show the observed CDF of our 21 V z -GAL DSFGs considered for the analysis in this paper (Table 2 ). The observed inclination distribution shows a moderate deviation from the expectation for randomly oriented disks (Kolmogorov-Smirnov or KS statistics; D = 0.34 D=0.34 and p = 0.012 p=0.012 ), which would formally reject the null hypothesis of random orientations at the ( ∼ 2.5 ​ σ \sim 2.5\sigma ) level. However, when measurement uncertainties in the axis ratios and derived inclinations are propagated through Monte Carlo realizations, the median KS test probability increases to ( p = 0.061 p=0.061 ) (16th-84th percentile range: 0.02–0.16). Therefore, the evidence against a random inclination distribution is weakened considerably, and the current sample of 21 galaxies remains at best only marginally inconsistent with random orientations. Furthermore, the inferred inclinations are not direct observables but are derived from dust-continuum axis ratios under assumptions regarding the intrinsic disk thickness ( q 0 \rm q_{0} ) and the correspondence between dust morphology and disk orientation. Given these additional systematic uncertainties, the current data do not provide compelling evidence against a random orientation distribution, and the hypothesis of randomly oriented disks cannot be robustly rejected. 25 25 25 Note also that dust geometry may not truly represent the cold gas disk and its inclination. sections.heading: VII.6 Contributors to the Dynamical Mass Uncertainties and “ α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} Tension”
sections.text: In the absence of resolved cold gas data, the dynamical mass estimation using the proposed “mixed” (i.e., rotating, turbulent, thick-disk) estimator in Eqn. 8 involves four key observables, namely inclination and CO(1–0) FWHM for v rot v_{\rm rot} , velocity dispersion, and radius. In Figure 19 , we quantitatively show the contributions of uncertainty in each of these parameters that can propagate to the inferred dynamical upper limits on the α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} . As expected, α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} is more sensitive to the CO(1–0) line FWHM and inclination angle — both contributing through the rotational velocity assumption — followed by radius being the next large uncertainty. Dynamical mass constraints have often favored α CO = 0.8 \alpha_{\rm CO}=0.8 M ⊙ ​ ( K ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ pc 2 ) − 1 \rm M_{\odot}~{(K~km~{s}^{-1}~{pc}^{2})}^{-1} , whereas dust- and radiative-transfer-based methods imply higher values.
