For 12 galaxies with robust modeling constraints, we derive molecular gas masses using dust spectral energy distribution modeling and the TUNER LVG framework, adopting a solar-metallicity gas-to-dust mass ratio of 100. Although not fully independent due to shared assumptions on dust properties, these approaches yield mutually consistent gas masses corresponding to α CO ∼ 1.5 − 11.5 \alpha_{\rm CO}\sim 1.5-11.5 M ⊙ ​ ( K ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ pc 2 ) − 1 \rm M_{\odot}~{(K~km~{s}^{-1}~{pc}^{2})}^{-1} , with a median near the Galactic α CO = 4.3 \alpha_{\rm CO}=4.3 M ⊙ ​ ( K ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ pc 2 ) − 1 \rm M_{\odot}~{(K~km~{s}^{-1}~{pc}^{2})}^{-1} . Isotropic virial dynamical masses agree with these gas masses when realistic molecular gas sizes are adopted, while our proposed “mixed” (rotating, pressure-supported, thick-disk) estimator systematically underestimates dynamical masses, producing low α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} limits. Using GN20 ( z = 4.055 z=4.055 ) as a case study, we show that resolved gas geometry and kinematics reconcile the discrepancy with LVG-derived α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} . Our results suggest that current data do not require α CO = 0.8 ​ M ⊙ ​ ( K ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ pc 2 ) − 1 \alpha_{\rm CO}=0.8~\rm M_{\odot}~(K~km~s^{-1}~pc^{2})^{-1} , and intermediate to near-Galactic values remain dynamically viable given uncertainties in gas geometry, dust properties, and gas-to-dust ratios. Further progress in calibrating α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} in the early universe will require resolved molecular gas observations, physically motivated ISM modeling, and stringent constraints on dust properties. Keywords: galaxies: high-redshift — CO line emission — molecular gas — galaxies: kinematics and dynamics — radiative transfer show]prajapati@ph1.uni-koeln.de I Introduction Cold molecular gas is a fundamental component in the formation and evolution of galaxies across cosmic time [ 85 , 80 , 100 , 103 ] . Commonly traced via 12 C 16 O — hereafter, CO — rotational transitions, it both fuels star formation and serves as a sensitive probe of galactic gas dynamics. CO(1–0), with ν rest = 115.271 \rm\nu_{rest}=115.271 GHz, is the ground-state rotational transition and can be excited even in the most extended, cold gas reservoirs. CO(1–0) line luminosities, L CO ⁡ ( 1 − 0 ) ′ L^{\prime}_{\rm CO(1-0)} (in units of K ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ pc 2 \rm K~km~{s}^{-1}~{pc}^{2} ) are, therefore, commonly used to derive total molecular gas masses ( M H 2 M_{\rm H_{2}} ) via the CO–H 2 conversion factor [ 90 , α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} in units of M ⊙ ​ ( K ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ pc 2 ) − 1 \rm M_{\odot}~{(K~km~{s}^{-1}~{pc}^{2})}^{-1} ; see] . M H 2 ​ [ M ⊙ ] = α CO ​ L CO ⁡ ( 1 − 0 ) ′ M_{\rm H_{2}}\,{\rm[M_{\odot}]}=\alpha_{\rm CO}\,\,L^{\prime}_{\rm CO(1-0)} (1) Within the Milky Way and nearby main-sequence galaxies, α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} is known to vary with local physical conditions, including temperature, density, and metallicity [ 67 , 59 , e.g.,] . However, direct, non-dynamical estimates of the α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} conversion factor in the local universe are themselves subject to significant systematic uncertainties. Calibrations based on γ \gamma -ray emission, visual and infrared extinction, X-ray absorption, dust emission, and isotopologue measurements generally agree at ∼ \sim 15–25% level, but exhibit an overall spread approaching a factor of about 2 in some environments [ 66 , see e.g.,] . Importantly, these differences are not purely statistical but appear to be systematically offset between methods, suggesting that residual physical and methodological uncertainties remain even in nearby systems where such calibrations are most applicable. On galaxy-integrated scales, additional uncertainty is expected due to the optical thickness of the low- J CO transitions, which can produce intrinsic variations in CO emissivity across different gas phases and environments [ 8 ] . Such effects are already evident in resolved observations of local molecular clouds and complexes [ 63 , e.g.,] . On the other hand, local ultra-luminous infrared galaxies or ULIRGs and high- z dusty star-forming galaxies (DSFGs) rarely have direct measurements of α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} . Instead, their α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} is typically inferred from unresolved, global CO observations and indirect constraints, relying on assumptions about gas geometry, excitation conditions, dynamics, gravitationally supported motions, and virialization that may break down in extreme star-forming environments [ 8 , 39 ] . A long-standing result from these approaches is that submillimeter-bright dusty systems across redshifts appear to convert gas into stars more rapidly than coeval main-sequence galaxies, implying short depletion times and highly efficient star formation such as that seen in local ULIRGs/mergers [ 38 , 5 , 46 , 76 , e.g.,] . In the same systems, masses inferred from dynamical constraints using integrated CO linewidths are often lower than the molecular gas masses obtained from CO luminosity when adopting a Milky Way-calibrated α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} , implying that a systematically lower inferred CO–H 2 conversion factor is appropriate for ULIRGs and DSFGs [ 27 , 2 , e.g.,] . This discrepancy is commonly referred to as the “ α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} tension”. A key open question is whether the apparent tension between galaxy-integrated molecular gas masses inferred from CO luminosities and dynamical constraints reflects genuine variations in the physical conversion factor across populations or instead arises from observational limitations. While studies of nearby molecular clouds and ULIRGs generally benefit from well-constrained dynamics, remaining discrepancies there may instead reflect assumptions about the physical state of the gas (e.g., virial equilibrium or cloud structure). In contrast, high- z DSFGs are affected by substantially larger observational uncertainties. The absence of integrated CO(1–0) measurements in many studies introduces uncertainties associated with gas excitation corrections. Even when such data are available, complex kinematic structures — including rotation, turbulence, inflows/outflows, and merger-driven motions — are generally reduced to a single integrated linewidth. In addition, dynamical mass estimates depend on source sizes, geometry, and inclination, parameters that are often poorly constrained, thereby compounding the overall uncertainty. These quantities are typically inferred from resolved dust continuum morphology because directly imaging the cold molecular gas at comparable resolution remains observationally challenging. Altogether, these may systematically bias gas mass and dynamical estimates, making it difficult to determine whether the inferred global, low α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} values in high- z DSFGs are intrinsic or observationally driven. Spatially resolved observations of inherently faint CO(1–0) offer a direct way to break these degeneracies by independently constraining gas extent and kinematics for high- z DSFGs. However, such studies remain limited at high redshift due to sensitivity constraints. They are typically restricted to the brightest or strongly lensed galaxies and quasars [ 77 , 96 , 87 , e.g.,] , where interpretations may be affected by additional uncertainties from lensing reconstruction models. Existing high-resolution CO(1–0) and CO(2–1) studies of unlensed high- z DSFGs [ 39 , e.g.,] remain limited to only a handful of objects (e.g., GN20 at z ∼ 4 z\sim 4 ; Hodge et al. 49 ) and often lack the sensitivity required for robust dynamical modeling. Consequently, they have not yet determined whether the apparent low α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} values in high- z DSFGs arise primarily from observational limitations or reflect genuine physical variations. Discrepancies between the molecular gas mass estimates and dynamical constraints remain even when masses are inferred from integrated [CII] or (typically optically thin) [CI] observations 1 1 1 Assuming all C + or C is directly related to star formation, i.e., no formation due to shock compression. , lacking a systematic comparison of conversion factors across various tracers for large samples of DSFGs [ 29 , 32 , e.g.,] . This motivates a re-examination of the apparent α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} tension in high- z DSFGs, where observational limitations are likely to play a much larger role than in nearby systems. Quantifying the impact of unresolved kinematics and uncertain source sizes is essential for determining whether these observational biases largely drive the low conversion factors inferred for current high- z statistical samples or whether a residual discrepancy remains after improved dynamical constraints are obtained. A previous study of homogeneously selected unlensed, high- z DSFGs reports 11 robust CO(1–0) detections [ 38 ] . Further, a handful of additional CO(1–0) studies of unlensed galaxies exist, such as [ 15 , 55 , 88 , 58 ] . To address limitations arising from heterogeneous selection effects and limited statistics, the VLA V z -GAL CO(1--0) large program 2 2 2 vzgal.uni-koeln.de [ 93 , 76 ] has studied CO(1–0) emission in 106 Herschel/SPIRE 500 μ \mu m-selected high- z DSFGs. These 106 sources were selected from a parent sample of 135 DSFGs detected in higher- J CO lines and far-infrared continuum by the NOEMA z -GAL survey [ 22 ] . In this paper, we focus on the unlensed sources identified at z = 1 − 6 z=1-6 within the V z -GAL sample. In Section II , we describe the identification of the target sample and available data. In Section III , we analyze the data to infer resolved dust sizes and inclination angles. We also derive their gas masses using two complementary methods, one using dust spectral energy distribution modeling and another involving a large velocity gradient model [ 104 , 10 , LVG; see] . Section IV explores an isotropic virial and a rotational thick-disk estimator of dynamical masses for DSFGs, and compares them to the molecular gas masses. 3 3 3 The dynamical constraints explored in this work should be interpreted in the context of a non-negligible intrinsic uncertainty floor in the standard CO–H 2 conversion factors, even in the local universe, alongside observational and modeling uncertainties in the gas mass and dynamical measurements. Assuming optically thin dust emission, Ismail et al. [54] modeled the integrated dust spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of the sample, while Berta et al. [5] studied the gas properties. For this paper, we visually classify a V z -GAL galaxy as gravitationally lensed if it satisfies one or both of the following criteria (see Figure 1 ): (i) the ALMA dust continuum exhibits clear lensing signatures, such as extended morphologies with arcs, rings, or Einstein crosses, and/or (ii) a foreground object is present along the line of sight in the HST imaging that could plausibly act as a lens for the DSFG in the background. Galaxies that instead display compact dust emission peak(s) and lack any evident foreground lensing source are classified as unlensed DSFGs (see also Appendix § \lx@sectionsign VII.1 ). II.3 V z -GAL CO(1–0) Measurements Unresolved measurements of the CO(1–0) emission-line fluxes for our targets were presented in the V z -GAL studies [ 93 , 76 ] . All the 21 DSFGs selected here have > 3 ​ σ >3\sigma detection of the CO(1–0) line. Table 2 summarizes their FWHM and CO(1–0) line luminosities adopted from the V z -GAL papers. The overall spread in CO(1–0) line luminosities of our sources is consistent with that found in the literature for high- z DSFGs or submillimeter galaxies (SMGs) [ 2 , 38 , e.g.,] . CO(1–0) emission for most of the 21 targets can be well described by a single Gaussian profile with an FWHM of 300 to 700 km s − 1 \rm{s}^{-1} . Similar linewidths have also been observed in the literature for other unlensed SMGs/DSFGs [ 15 , 38 , e.g.,] . A few of our systems, however, show more complex CO(1–0) line profiles (Appendix § \lx@sectionsign VII.2 ). • HeLMS-32C, HeLMS-50, HerBS-43a, and HerBS-43b show double-peaked CO(1–0) line profiles. All except HeLMS-50 are nearly symmetric, and the spatial distribution of dust emission in all of them appears compact. • HeLMS-50, HerBS-43a, HerBS-188, and HerBS-191 show broad (FWHM ≳ \gtrsim 1000 km s − 1 {\rm s}^{-1} ) CO(1–0) line profiles. Their resolved dust emission does not show any clear merger signatures. Moreover, HeLMS-50, HerBS-43a, HerBS-43b, and HerBS-191 exhibit dust radii larger than 3 kpc ( § \lx@sectionsign III.1.1 ), leading to their total dust extents spanning beyond ∼ \sim 6 kpc. For all systems displaying complex CO(1--0) line profiles, the lack of obvious merger signatures in the current ALMA dust-continuum maps, however, does not rule out ongoing or past merger activity, particularly if such features are obscured by projection effects. 4 4 4 We also expect that deeper, multi-array-configuration dust observations would further help reveal more extended dust emission in all sources. III.1.1 Dust Radii and Axis Ratios We assume that the dust is distributed in a circular, inclined disk-like morphology, whose size ( R dust R_{\rm dust} ) is thus best represented by the major axis size of the dust emission; i.e., R dust = r major {R}_{\mathrm{dust}}=r_{\mathrm{major}} . Most sources in our sample have dust-emitting radii between 1–3 kpc (Figure 3 ), with a sample median radius of 2.2 ± 0.4 2.2\pm 0.4 kpc. Only 5/21 sources (HeLMS-50, HerBS-43a, HerBS-43b, HerBS-70E, and HerBS-191) exhibit radii above 3 kpc. Among these, HerBS-191 is the most extended source with a dust-emitting radius ∼ \sim 7 kpc. Based on the minor and major axis sizes listed in Table 1 , we derive the observed axis ratios q = r minor / r major q=r_{\rm minor}/r_{\rm major} spanning 0.4–0.9, with a median value of 0.6 ± 0.1 0.6\pm 0.1 . The median axis ratio and overall range are comparable between 6/21 sources ( § \lx@sectionsign II.3 ) with complex CO(1–0) line profiles and the rest with a single Gaussian-like line profile. The observed range of axis ratios reveals a broad diversity in projected dust morphologies, from nearly circular to highly elongated. III.1.2 Dust versus Cold Molecular Gas Sizes The median dust radius of 2.2 kpc for our sample is about 3 × 3\times lower than previously assumed [ 12 ] or previously observed [ 78 , 55 , 49 ] low- J CO radii of 7 kpc in the literature. For a given galaxy, the dust continuum size is expected to be lower than the cold gas size due to the radiative-transfer effects [ 14 , 10 , e.g.,] involving spatial variations in gas column density, temperature, and optical depth (see Appendix § \lx@sectionsign VII.3 ). This is true even in the absence of plausible biases coming from the observational constraints. Therefore, dust sizes may not necessarily trace the entire cold molecular gas disk; instead, they may represent a relatively compact region near the center, e.g., a bulge or a bar. James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observations of high- z unlensed DSFGs already confirm that their active star formation extends beyond the central bulges traced by dust [ 50 ] . Since dynamical masses ( M dyn ∝ radius M_{\rm dyn}\propto{\rm radius} ; see § \lx@sectionsign IV.1 and § \lx@sectionsign IV.2 ), adopting dust continuum sizes may therefore yield systematically lower dynamical masses than would be inferred using the full CO(1--0) extent. 5 5 5 We emphasize here that although CO(1–0) is generally optically thick and therefore does not linearly trace molecular column density, its luminosity remains correlated with molecular gas mass via α CO \alpha_{\rm CO} because, in the galaxy-scale observations, the velocity-integrated emission from ensembles of turbulent, self-gravitating molecular clouds scales approximately with the total molecular mass [ 26 , 91 , 8 , e.g.,] .
